title: 'Surprised We Are Still Alive': AIIMS Doctor Warns Delhi Air Is Poisonous
excerpt: AIIMS professor Vijay Hadda says even healthy colleagues cannot shake throat irritation from Delhi's post-Diwali air, and that green crackers cut emissions by only about 30 per cent.
body:
• Dr Vijay Hadda, Professor of Pulmonary Medicine and Sleep Disorders at AIIMS, said of Delhi's post-Diwali air: "I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival."
  • Doctors at AIIMS and Apollo Hospitals say even healthy people, including adults aged 20 to 50, are reporting throat irritation, coughing and breathlessness — not only patients with existing lung or heart disease.
  • Apollo's Dr S Chatterjee said symptoms can begin within four to six hours of exposure at severe pollution levels and can continue afterwards, so residents should avoid unnecessary outdoor activity and outdoor exercise while levels stay high.
  • Hadda said green crackers cut emissions by only about 30 per cent, with 70 per cent of gases and particulate matter comparable to conventional firecrackers.

Delhi's post-Diwali pollution has drawn an unusually blunt warning from one of the capital's senior lung specialists. Dr Vijay Hadda, Professor in the Department of Pulmonary Medicine and Sleep Disorders at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), said continuous exposure to the city's air was posing a serious challenge to everyone living in the capital, according to ANI reporting carried by Devdiscourse.

"You keep inhaling this poisonous smoke, breathing it in continuously. Every minute, you breathe at least 20 times, taking in at least half a litre of air with each breath. I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival."

— Dr Vijay Hadda, Professor of Pulmonary Medicine and Sleep Disorders, AIIMS

Hadda said the AQI, which earlier remained in three digits, had now reached four digits, and that the effects of prolonged exposure would become increasingly visible. Patients seen in an outpatient session had returned again with symptoms, he said, and colleagues with no health problems were calling him about throat irritation they could not shake. "Many of my colleagues who are otherwise completely healthy have been calling me and saying, 'I am unable to get rid of this irritation. It feels as though something is stuck in my throat,'" he said, in coverage also summarised by Saptashwa TV.

Healthy people are reporting symptoms too

Dr S Chatterjee, Senior Consultant in Internal Medicine at Apollo Hospitals, said doctors were receiving complaints not only from people with existing lung or heart conditions but also from otherwise healthy individuals. "Healthy people with no underlying illnesses are complaining of symptoms. Young people in the 20–50 age group are also experiencing these problems, and that is what worries me," Chatterjee said. "We always expect people with lung or cardiac diseases to experience such symptoms when the AQI is this high. However, even healthy individuals are reporting symptoms."

Chatterjee warned that the impact could extend beyond the immediate pollution episode. "When you are exposed to such high levels of AQI or such severe pollution, symptoms can begin to appear even in otherwise healthy individuals within four to six hours. But the effects do not stop there. They will continue. Therefore, the next few days are going to be very important for the healthcare system," he said. He advised people to avoid unnecessary outdoor exposure, including shopping, and to refrain from exercising outdoors while pollution levels are high.

Green crackers are not pollution-free

Hadda also questioned the idea that green firecrackers solve the Diwali emissions problem. "These green crackers reduce emissions by only 30%. As far as the gases and particulate matter are concerned, 70% of the emissions remain the same as those from conventional firecrackers," he said.

Delhi's citywide AQI was recorded at 368 at 7 a.m. on Monday, November 9, in the "very poor" category, with several monitoring stations above 400, in the "severe" range, according to Central Pollution Control Board data reported across outlets. Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan remained in force across Delhi-NCR.

A crisis that returns every year

Hadda pointed to the recurring pattern as part of the problem. "This happens every year, but somehow, we all forget. The general public forgets, and even policies remain somewhat in a grey area, making it difficult to understand how they should be interpreted. Overall, the situation is not good at all. You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it," he said.

For diaspora readers with parents and family in the capital, the doctors' advice is direct: limit time outdoors while levels stay severe, skip outdoor exercise, and treat a cough or throat irritation that does not settle as a reason to see a doctor rather than wait it out.
